claims.text: The starting material is a binder-containing green body printed from blended elemental metal oxides intended to form an HEA.
Binder jetting or ink-extrusion followed by tailored co-reduction sintering under a reducing atmosphere can progressively reduce the oxide feedstock.
An optimized co-reduction profile will leave less residual oxide, particularly unreduced Cr2O3, than a standard non-optimized process.
De-binding should precede oxide reduction and sintering.
The constituent oxides reduce sequentially, with Co, Fe, and Ni oxides reducing at lower temperature than Cr2O3.
Hydrogen or another suitable reducing gas can be used to reduce compatible oxide feedstocks.
A suitable temperature profile can achieve full oxide reduction while avoiding excessive grain growth.
Unreduced Cr2O3 decreases contact between metallic particles and acts as a local diffusion and sintering barrier.
Reduction of Cr2O3 to metallic Cr allows Cr to diffuse into and alloy with the surrounding metal matrix.
Removing residual oxide barriers promotes interparticle bonding and matrix homogeneity.
Controlling reduction kinetics produces more rapid and uniform interdiffusion of metallic species.
Reduction of oxide barriers promotes densification and lowers porosity.
The optimized route will reduce dimensional distortion during fabrication.
The optimized route will yield lower overall porosity and fewer large pores than conventional beam-based AM or non-optimized binder-based processing.
The optimized route will improve dimensional accuracy relative to conventional beam-based AM or non-optimized binder-based processing.
The optimized route will increase strength and ductility relative to conventional beam-based AM or non-optimized binder-based processing.
The intervention should transfer to HEA oxide feedstocks having similar compositions and reduction kinetics.
The intervention may be less effective when constituent oxides require radically different reduction profiles.
Binder contaminants may interfere with oxide-reduction kinetics.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in dimensional accuracy, porosity, and mechanical properties relative to a control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The experiment proposes using the same oxide-based feedstock for a conventional beam-based AM control, while the stated process concept and cited evidence distinguish oxide-ink processing from conventional beam-based processing, which ordinarily uses elemental or pre-alloyed metal powder. The alternative non-optimized binder-based control avoids this mismatch, but the control definition remains ambiguous.
